utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think so. Yes, for sure. We came on the 3rd and we left on the 4th. We could not actually leave on the 3rd, because there were no buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you go to leave? Was it the bus station?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: There was a bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were there other people trying to leave Foca at that time, on the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I think there were about a thousand of us there, and about 530 or something like that, about 530 of us got onto these four buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these thousand, were they Muslims people or were they people of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Primarily Muslims. Only the town police was at the bridge by the station, and also over there by the department store. These soldiers were passing by us. They were shooting above us, cursing at us, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these soldiers, do you know which unit they came from?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were Muslim or Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you travelled and you left Foca on the 4th of July, 1992, and you travelled to another country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, to Montenegro, and then through Montenegro to Serbia, and from Serbia to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: May I introduce myself. I am Miroslav Vasic and I'm one of the counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac. I'd like to ask you first, because we speak the same language, to make the job easier slightly for the interpreters, so will you please pause after you hear my question so as to avoid us speaking on top of each other. Thank you. Today you answered my learned friend in response to his question, and you spoke about the events in Pilipovici in 1992 and you said that people had sought shelter in the army depot which was there. Could you tell us if those were local people from Pilipovici there?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: No, not all of them were from Pilipovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: They were people from Pilipovici and they were also people from Foca, from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about how White Eagles had come and taken you out of the hangar and that on that occasion Mr. Salko Sehovic and Mr. Meho Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dedovic were killed. Could you tell me, if you know, why they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the members of that unit which had come read out from some lists. What was on those lists? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes, they did read names of some people, but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you, in your statement to the OTP, say that you thought that those lists contained the members of the SDA? Will you just wait for the interpretation to end, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the witness said "probably."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And persons who were killed, were they related in some way or the other to those people who were on the lists, allegedly members of the SDA, as you say?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. Maybe their children or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, it is very important that you give more time to the interpreters to catch up before you answer the question. Just wait a little bit longer, and then the interpreters will be able to catch up. It's always very difficult for them when you're both speaking the same language. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I could suggest -- perhaps I -- because I can follow the interpretation in English, perhaps I could tell the witness when he should answer, because he does not speak English. Perhaps that will resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know how you propose to do that, Mr. Vasic. Are you going to flag him? Let's see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say, "Yes, will you go ahead." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that on that occasion, people who were killed had been taken some ten metres away. Could you tell us in what direction? Were they taken behind the hangar or -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Right behind us. To the right from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that occasion, did the members of the White Eagles break your eyeglasses?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, they took my eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Will you wait, please, for the interpretation? I will tell you "go ahead" when the interpretation is over.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you have any difficulty with colours, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do have difficulties with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That is, you cannot distinguish colours?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I distinguish some. I know some and I don't others. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me the [indiscernible] of your eyeglasses?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me -- you described today your detention in the KP Dom. While you were in the KP Dom, were you ill-treated physically, beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, before I arrived in the KP Dom, not in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today, you spoke about the prohibition of movement which applied to Muslims in the town when you left the KP Dom. And you also said that the policeman had told you to take the shortest way back home. Can you tell me if the prohibition was introduced perhaps to protect the Muslims? Was it safe for Muslims to move about the streets which were full of troops and police?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Strange question, strange question, that it was for our safety. To kill people and you call that safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Because you said that the policeman had told to you take the shortest way back because it was not safe to move about the town; that is why I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, it depended on so that I wouldn't see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tell the OTP investigator, at the time when you made your statement in 1995, that Colonel Kovac was the chief commander of the Chetnik Crisis Centre, of the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he -- who was his deputy, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Simo Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you see that Simo Stanojevic was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Foca before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Are you familiar with the name Sulejman Pilav?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I've heard it, but I don't really know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Sulejman Pilav was in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You told us today that when you came to the KP Dom, you noticed guards wearing the same uniforms as the guards before the war. After that, you said that you had never been to the KP Dom before the war. Can you then explain how do you know what kind of uniforms did the guards in the KP Dom have before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: You know how?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Will you please wait until the interpretation is finished? Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: You know how I know? Because before the war, the guards bought their uniforms like now during the war, and I knew it because they came up there where I worked. That is, the detainees from the KP Dom came to work there, and guards were escorting them, so I could see the difference between the town police and the guards, because there was a slight difference in their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You told us today about your arrival in the KP Dom, how you arrived there in a bus escorted by soldiers who had brought you from Pilipovici and how they turned you over to the guards in the KP Dom. And you said that a guard asked, "Have they been searched?" And then you said that somebody said, "Take them in." Can you tell us who was it that said that?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: That soldier who had brought us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your detention in KP Dom, did you see any soldiers in the compound or around the buildings?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Mr. Taib Rahman today and you told us how you knew that he had been injured because he was in your room. Could you tell me, when was he taken out?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I can't, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was he brought back to your room?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, that same day, the day that they took him out, that same day they brought him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But did you see him being taken away and coming back?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I did, because the guard entered, called out his name, took him out, and the guard brought him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know which guard was that?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spoke about a detainee with an injury to his head. Could you tell us, where did you see that detainee?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: In the room, in my room, in the room that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what was his name? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you that. I've forgotten his name. I did know what his name was. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke today about how you listened to the radio and that, among other things, you heard on the radio that the Muslims could not move about. Could you tell us if you also heard whether there was a curfew in Foca at the time, for all townsmen, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Only Muslims were prohibited to go out. The radio station explicitly said Muslims are prohibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that flats owned by people of Serb origin in your building had not been searched. Before that you told us that you only went out to report to the police. Could you then explain it to us how is it that you know that those flats were not searched?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Because I went past them to the police every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And how long would it take you to go from your flat through that building and to the police and back?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, as long as it took me to go down -- to walk down the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long did it take you?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know, the seventh floor. You can calculate it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of that time that it took you to walk down and walk up, you concluded on the basis of that that the Serb flats were not searched, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, of course they were not searched, because some Serbs, neighbours, came to my place, and they told me, and that was what they told me, that they had not been searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today when asked by my learned friend, you said that you were not a member of the SDA. Is that correct, or were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you a supporter of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know that much about their role either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in the multiparty elections, did you vote for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: Maybe I did, maybe I didn't. I don't exactly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the OTP investigator in 1995, did you tell him that in the elections of 1991 you voted for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I say, maybe I did, but I don't know. It was a long time ago. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I shall read to you the sentence from your statement that you gave on the 4th and 5th of May, 1995, to the OTP investigator. It is ID93 and ID93A, and it says, in the third line, that is, the third passage: "I was not a member of any of the new political parties. In the elections of 1991 I voted for the SDA." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I suppose I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: Since you were not an SDA member or supporter, why did you then vote for the SDA in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I'd rather not answer that kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it the national polarisation on both sides, amongst the Serbs and the Muslims, at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: I'd also not answer that question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you're not wearing glasses today. Does that mean that you only use glasses for reading?

utterances.speaker: JUSO TARANIN
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I have them here. But only when I have to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is the end of your evidence. We are grateful to you for coming here to give that evidence. You are free to leave, but would you wait a moment whilst the blinds are being lowered so that you can leave without the public seeing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is 146 and he has a pseudonym and image alteration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet will be Exhibit P428 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in the document that you are being handed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Excellency, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In front of you there is a sheet of paper, and that is Exhibit P428. On it you will see FWS-146. Beneath that, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: After your name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You no longer need to refer to that piece of paper. Witness, in 1992, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We lived in Rancici, Cajnice municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you married and did you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Married, four children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I was a worker, blue-collar, in my firm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what ethnicity are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992, did you have a particular medical condition that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. required hospitalisation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990 I began to suffer from asthma.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On April 1st, 1992, were you admitted to the hospital for asthma?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Which hospital was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Internal medicine ward, Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What kind of treatment did you receive?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They treated me super, and Dr. Milena had all the medicines, and that is where I was admitted and treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you required to stay overnight in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed there, and I was treated there for six months in the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: At the beginning, when you were admitted to the hospital, were you told that you would be there for six months' treatment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. The doctor said, "We shall see if the ambulance from Gorazde comes. Then we shall try to send you to Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let me back up a little bit there. While you were receiving treatment in Foca hospital, did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: After seven days, the war started in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the fact that the war started have an effect on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I had medicines and I was treated. I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did people come to the hospital to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. When there was this aggression, when the war broke out, the hospital was practically full.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The people who sought shelter at the hospital, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: It didn't matter. There were Serbs, there were Muslims. We were all together. Somebody took a car, somebody fled from the hospital when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did any soldiers come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I saw two kinds of soldiers when Foca fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When did Foca fall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, Foca fell -- I came on the 1st of April, so it was after Bajram, around the 12th day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said you saw two kinds of soldiers. What were the two kinds?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, in uniform, some kind of White Eagles. There were songs. Then also the Foca Chetniks, and uniforms of the former JNA, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did the soldiers do when they came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Nothing. They sang. They would carry a one-litre bottle of brandy in their hands. They would walk around a bit and leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the soldiers take over the hospital or set up anything at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The hospital was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: It was already taken. Basically, I wouldn't dare to move about. There was shooting. Foca was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I understand that you were not able to move about because there was a war going on in Foca. Who was in charge of the hospital after Foca fell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I can't remember. I was sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did any soldiers set up any sort of artillery at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to see any shooting coming from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: If I had been able to go to the terrace, I actually did go and I saw that Foca was on fire, that there was shooting, and I went back to bed because my health was the most important of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see a civilian or military truck get shot at?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, I just happened to go out on the terrace and I saw a kombi van coming from the direction of Foca. It had set out for Gorazde. It hadn't passed even a kilometre. In front of the hospital, there was a machine-gun nest and they shot at the car from that nest, and I saw the kombi van veer from the road, and it stopped there, and we heard moaning, and then the ambulance came. There were some people who were wounded. And then they were transferred to hospital. And I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell whether the people in the van were wearing military uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, you couldn't tell or they were not wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I couldn't see. It was far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was the kombi van itself a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No, civilian. These were civilians who had set out for Gorazde, practically to flee. That's what I basically heard later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you said the people inside that van were taken to hospital, were they brought to the Foca hospital where you were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The Foca hospital was where I was treated, where I lay, but I was at the internal medicine ward and then there was this other building where they took them in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Foca hospital, was the entire medical staff -- did the entire medical staff stay working at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Of course, the staff stayed there to work. I had medicine and my treatment continued. I was still treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The staff that continued to treat you, were they Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the Muslim staff?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, cars came from Gorazde. They made phone calls, or people, Muslim people, would cross the Drina on foot over the bridge, and they would run away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: My question was focused on the medical staff. Your description, was that of the patients or of the medical staff, the Muslims patients or the Muslim medical staff ran away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: As regards the humaneness of doctors and medical staff, they were humane, they still treated us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to clarify this line of questioning. Witness, you said that the staff that treated you were Serb. Right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were first admitted to the hospital, were you treated by Serb and Muslim doctors or at that time already were you treated only by Serb doctors?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Please, I came to hospital on the 1st of April, 1992. I was received by this lady doctor, Milena, at the internal ward where I was treated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a time when the Muslim staff and doctors were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But do you know that they were taken away from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Later I heard that there's no Muslim people, that they took some from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim patients? You said you stayed at the hospital. What happened to the other Muslim patients?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. They worked for about a month or two, but then you would just see all of a sudden that there were no Muslim patients and no Muslim doctors in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many Muslim patients were left with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you said you remained at the hospital for six months?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During those six months were any attempts made for you to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. The first time we were taken practically to Trnovo in the ambulance vehicle that was used for kidney treatment. The three of us were taken for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why you weren't released at that point?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The doctor said that if I were to be exchanged, that I should be taken to Sarajevo, and if we were not to be exchanged, that we should come back to the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said you were taken almost to Trnovo. Did you actually reach Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We came to Trnovo on the 27th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What caused you to turn around and go back to the Foca hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We arrived in Trnovo. We got out. Another kombi van came. We got into that kombi van and then we went back to Foca. We passed a hundred metres and then we got into the water, into a stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you return to the Foca hospital on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. We waited for orders until nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what happened at nightfall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Then we got orders. They blindfolded us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Then they drove us for about half an hour. There was some kind of a kombi van. We went out. There was some kind of headquarters, and they put us into a garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to? Were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Soldiers. Soldiers came out and they put us up at a garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that garage?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We spent the night in the garage. In the morning we got breakfast and their doctor examined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Then they said to us, "It's all in vain. There is shooting around Sarajevo." The people who were to be exchanged didn't come, so then we were returned to the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you gave the date of this as the 27th July 1993. Is that the right date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The 27th of July, 1993, the exact date. It was hot. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were in the hospital -- are you talking about when you were taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were in the hospital in 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So did this happen in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Oh, 1992 - I'm so sorry - I was taken from hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was there another time when you were taken out of the hospital but returned and not released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, when we were returned from Trnovo. About a month later, a nurse came and told us that we should get ready because the last buses were about to leave for Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And were you taken to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. Again, the telephone, and they told us that we can stay, because the buses were full. So we remained in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was there another time when you were supposed to be released from the hospital but were not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We were supposed to go to Montenegro, to Prijepolje, in an ambulance vehicle that's used for kidney treatment, but the papers had not been prepared, so we remained in hospital again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did your family know that you were in the hospital during this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They knew that I went to Foca, because my doctor, Milan Tupesa, from the company where I worked in, sent me to hospital on the 1st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why you were not just released, like the other patients, to go to your family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Allegedly there was shooting, and the lady doctor said that if an ambulance would come from Gorazde, then I could be transferred. However, nothing came out of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During the six months that you remained at Foca hospital, did you hear shooting in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I did hear shooting. Foca was practically on fire. The villages around Foca were on fire. There was fear, there was panic, uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was there a time when Serb patients, a large group of Serb soldiers, was brought to the hospital for treatment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Six months later I saw a military man drying his uniform on the terrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did that indicate to you, that he was a patient there or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Nothing. He didn't ask us a thing. Of course, we thought that patients were brought into hospital and that they were lying in bed like the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In September of 1992, was there a group of about 35 Serb soldiers brought to the hospital who had been injured?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: When I could walk around and take a glass of juice, I saw there were about 20 wounded persons. I don't know whether it was from mines or because of the shooting. I don't know. I just saw wounded soldiers that were being brought into hospital. I would hear sirens and there would be killed and wounded persons, but I couldn't see what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said this was at a point when you could walk around. Approximately what month was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: That was already the fourth month after I had recuperated, actually, when I had been receiving drips and oxygen, and I could then start moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So was it approximately September 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I was in hospital, in bed, from the 1st of April until September, for six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What date were you finally -- were you taken away from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: On the 2nd of October, 1992, after the lady doctor came to see me, and a Serb soldier came in. And there were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was that Serb soldier? Did you recognise him or learn his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He spoke loudly. He had a beard. He followed the lady doctor after she had come to examine us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He said to the doctor, "Fuck you. Why you feeding balijas? If you were a man, I'd kill you right now." And he grabbed his pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did the soldier do with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He pointed it at the lady doctor and she said, "Pero, may your children be alive. I'm a doctor. And by the lives of your children, these are patients, Muslims, who are very sick, and I'm a doctor and I'm supposed to treat people."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did the soldier respond?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Then he used chairs and beat the three of us with -- and kicked us too, and two of my ribs were broken and four teeth kicked out. However, the doctor ran out of the room and phoned the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the police arrive?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Police arrived. The nurse wiped the blood off us and offered -- and told us to get ready, as soon as possible, and to come with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We got ready and started going downstairs. The two of them were in front of me and I was behind them. I walked very slowly. I was in pain. A Serb policeman hit me with a baton on the back. Had it not been for the railing, I would have fallen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said the policeman. Was this civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: An ordinary policeman. Later, he kicked me all the time too, on our way out, all the way to the car. When we got out, I don't know what he hit me with but I know that I fell and that my nose started to bleed. The medical staff were outside sitting on the bench, smoking, and they screamed, "Oh, what's happening to (redacted)?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you gave a statement to the Bosnian authorities in November, 1994, you didn't mention that the police hit or kicked you when they took you out of the hospital. Can you explain why you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I didn't dare. I was afraid, panic-striken. There was no one to tell. There was a war on. There was panic. And then these two guys got into the car. They sat in the car, whereas the police opened the trunk and threw me into the trunk. Had there been a longer way, a longer ride, from the hospital to where they were taking me, I would have suffocated in there. There was dust, some kind of chains.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: After you were released in Sarajevo, two years later, you -- did you tell the authorities then about being hit by the policeman? You described being hit by the soldier but did you describe that the policeman had mistreated you on the way out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No, only Pero. Not two years; two and a half years. After two and a half years, I was exchanged in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Can you explain why you did not tell -- did not say at that time, two and a half years later, that the policeman had hit you in addition to Pero?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I didn't know the name, and I couldn't talk when I found out the name, I mean about Pero, but I don't know about this other one. I don't know the name of this man who was hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever learn Pero's last name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: When I got out of the prison, my doctor sent me to Fojnica. I went out to buy a newspaper, Dnevni Avaz, and I found a picture of this Pero. I heard that he got killed. His people said in the newspapers that he was a hero. Maybe you have that picture in that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you remember his last name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Elez.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where did the policemen take you that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: On that day, we were taken to the KP Dom prison from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were all three of you taken, the Muslim patients who remained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: All three of us, after six months, we were taken to the Foca prison, the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was your family ever notified that you had been taken from the hospital to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know where your family was during this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Caporancic [phoen], the municipality of Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with your family while were you in the hospital during those six months?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During the time that you were at KP Dom, were you allowed contact with your family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you learn later, after you were released, what your family thought had happened to you during this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They thought, basically, that they'd never see me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did they think that you had died?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at KP Dom? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They brought us to the gate, they handed us over to the guard. The guard asked where we had been. He searched me. We had pajamas and shaving kits. He took away my penknife, my pen, and registered all of this, but as he was asking us -- asking us, and in front of me, there was this man who was screaming because this other man was beating him, and he was yelling, "Merhaba. Merhaba." I was really afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where was this man being hit? In what part of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: At the entrance, at the gate, on the left-hand side, there were stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo, when he said that this man was screaming, "Merhaba," is that some identification matter that we have to concern ourselves with?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I was going to ask him what it meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We have just got to get it done fairly quickly so it doesn't go out in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Oh, no. It's not an identification matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Can you explain what the word you heard meant?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: That is a greeting, a Muslim greeting, that we use, "Merhaba" and "Selam Aleikum".

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Very well. It's 1.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to return very briefly to the time when you were at the Foca hospital. I asked you earlier whether there were Serb soldiers who were brought to be treated at the hospital. I'd like to ask you now whether there were Serb soldiers who died at the hospital, whether you saw coffins or bodies of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No, not in the hospital, but in front of the hospital there were wounded and dead and coffins.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was there one particular incident in September 1992 when a group of about 35 Serb soldiers were brought in dead or injured?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you later told by other detainees at KP Dom that there was a group of people taken out to pick plums in September of 1992 that was in retaliation for the death of a large number of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, that they were killed. Whether it was mines, I did not see, but our detainees were taken from the camp to pick plums, and these people have not returned yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you told what the relationship was between the soldiers who were killed by mines and the group of detainees taken out allegedly to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I did not hear that. I was ill. I could not go out. I don't know, and so I won't really talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the witness shown what has been placed in the trial binders as ID281. And for the Court's reference, and Defence counsel as well, ID281 consists of three separate documents. They are medical discharge forms, and the first one is dated beginning 1st of April, 1992. We'll just start with that one and I'll ask the witness to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Is that the medical discharge certificate from the Foca hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: This is the discharge document certificate from the hospital of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you'll notice that the date that it says you were -- you began your treatment at the hospital was 1st April 1992. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And then the date where it says you were treated until, there is a typewritten date and then it's crossed out and something is written over it by hand. Could you tell us what that typewritten date was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I can. This was typed in, and when we returned from Trnovo, the lady doctor, when she discharged me the second time, she changed this by hand, in a ballpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What was the typewritten date? If it's not clear on the copy, could you please let us know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No, it's not clear. I can't see it on the copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you have the originals of these discharge forms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you bring them with you to Court today?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I left them in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I think we may have a better copy in our folders.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I think you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd ask, with the assistance of the usher, that the witness be shown this copy. I think it's a little bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. This is clearer. 1st of April, 1992, 24th of April, that is when I was discharged from the hospital. And when I was brought back from Trnovo, I was admitted again. When I again went to the prison, the doctor changed the date that -- this was not the date when I left, and she used a pen to write two 7s.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So the date, 24th of April, was that the date that you were taken to Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I was taken to Trnovo on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you taken somewhere else, then, on the 24th of April, for exchange, and then brought back?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We were -- they had prepared us to go to Skopje, but we did not go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Then the date that was handwritten in, the 7th of July, 1992, were you taken away on that date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. On the 27th. That is when we were taken to Trnovo, on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So the 7 that is written in is meant to make what originally was typewritten as 24 into a 27 July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The 27th of July, which the doctor changed by hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show you the second document in ID281. This one. This document shows that the treatment began on the 9th of July, 1992 and lasted until the 15th of July. Can you tell us about those dates? Were you admitted back to the hospital on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I was readmitted, yes. We were two, three times brought back to the hospital. We went for exchange, were brought back again, and the doctor wrote the discharge certificate again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And finally the third part of ID281. This one shows your treatment beginning on the 9th of July and lasting until the 2nd of October, 1992. Is that right? And you'll see that the 2nd of October is also handwritten in over something else that was typewritten originally.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell what was typewritten underneath the 2nd of October?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I can't see that but the doctor did it by her own hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you supposed to have been released before October? And that was the date that was written -- that was typewritten underneath?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Must have been like that because the situation was such, the times were such, and the doctor, she prepared the discharge document because I could not get out. It must mean that she changed those dates by hand, using a ball-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes that ID281, which consists of three documents plus the English translations, be entered in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P281 and 281A. And it would have to go under seal, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And they will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, when you were taken to KP Dom, you described before the lunch break that you heard someone screaming and you started to describe where that was. You said to the left of the entrance. You described that there were stairs. Could you tell whether the sound was coming from upstairs, downstairs, or the same floor as the entrance?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: To the left from the ground floor, I heard screams and cries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell who was screaming or could you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you what was happening?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did that make you feel when you came in and heard that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Bad, illness, exhausted, and as a sick man sent to the KP Dom, to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What room were you taken to in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Number 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were the other two Muslim patients brought from the Foca hospital with you taken to that same room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: To the same room. All three of us were together in Room 15. The guard turned us over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us who those other patients were and what medical conditions they were suffering from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Abid Cocalic from Visegrad had a pacemaker built in, and Nezir Cengic from Miljevina, the village of Rataj. They were together with me, beaten, and together with me moved to the KP Dom, to the same room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what medical condition Nezir Cengic had?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The man came all black and blue, beaten. His face was black, beaten, brought from Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know for what reason Mr. Cengic was being treated in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were brought to the KP Dom, could you tell us what your medical condition was? Were you able to walk?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Very difficult. When I left the hospital, they gave me medicines, but I felt such pains in my rib cage that I could not barely walk from the reception room to my Room 15 in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the first few months in KP Dom, were you able to go to the canteen and eat with the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Not -- four months. They asked me. I was wrapped in a sheet in a corner, because I could not walk on my own two feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did you get food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: At times my detainees would bring my lunch and at times guards would do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you lose weight during the time you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I was 72 kilograms when I arrived and I was 57 when I left. I became shorter, smaller, and thinner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical treatment while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: We had medicines. I reported and I was given the medicines or the ambulance when I could not breathe. And they said to tell the guard when I needed it so that they can bring me a physician who would give me an injection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the guards bring you a physician to give you an injection?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. Later on Dr. Aziz Torlak and Ibro Karovic came to my room, and it was -- it became easier for me; that is, when I needed it, I had the injections and they gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You mentioned the two doctors, Dr. Torlak and Dr. Karovic came to your room. Did they come as detainees or as --

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did they come as detainees or as working doctors?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The same like detainees. They were also detained and they worked later on as doctors, helping both peoples, treating both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they detained in Room 15 with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. They arrived before me. I don't know which room. And then later on there were some exchanges and then they were brought to my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When they were brought to your room - that's what I want to clarify - were they brought to your room to be detained there or brought specifically to give you treatment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anybody try -- did either of those doctors try to secure your release from the KP Dom for medical reasons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I asked for a favour as a sick man, and they wrote some messages to the prison warden and the deputy warden, twice, written documents, but nothing came of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what they wrote in the documents?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They wrote my full name, sick man from the hospital; if there is a possibility, could he be exchanged before the envisaged time so that he could go to Gorazde as quickly as possible. But nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said that these notes were addressed to the warden and the deputy warden. Do you know what the names were? Were they addressed --

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I do not. I was ill. They did it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said that they were addressed to the warden and deputy warden. Were they addressed using those titles or were they addressed to specific named individuals?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They named it. They gave it to guards, and guards took it away. But nothing came out of those applications, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you know Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I did not leave the room. I did not work. I did not know. I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you anything about him, whether he worked at KP Dom, whether he had a function?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I heard from those detainees that there was a warden there, that there was a deputy there. The name I didn't learn because I was ill, and I have no way of knowing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you hear the name Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you -- let me ask you this. When you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in September 1998, you stated: "I think that Savo Todovic was the head of KP Dom. I never met him personally. I know that he had a deputy, but I forgot the name." Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I do, but that was a long time ago, and one can forget.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why or on what basis did you believe at that time that Savo Todovic was the head of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Because of my applications to do something with that and to see if I could be exchanged as quickly as possible, but nothing came out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were the requests for your exchange addressed to Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I think so. I think that both my applications were submitted, but nothing came out of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The question is specifically about Savo Todovic. Do you know whether the applications were addressed to him by name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Then on what basis did you believe, in 1998, that Savo Todovic was the head of KP Dom? Did someone tell you that? Did you actually see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I suppose so. I did not see him but I heard that name mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever have direct dealings with Savo Todovic, or indeed with the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With whom in the prison management or authority did you have dealings? Was it just the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Only the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a doctor Aziz Torlak. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He was in my room. He was taken away from my room in February or March at 11.00, and he is filed as missing to this day. He treated me because, when I received the fifth penicillin, I fell into a coma and he took my medical card and put -- and stamped it with his monogram. And I think it is on the basis of this monogram that he was registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said he was taken away. Who took him away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Policemen opened the door and said, "Dr. Torlak, get ready, you're to be exchanged." The doctor left and all trace of him has been lost since.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you gave the date as February, March. Would that be is 1993?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: 1993, because it says in my health card, "Chief Doctor, Torlak, Aziz Torlak, 20th of March, 1993." You can check it because you've got the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, we don't need much details on this particular point, but were you hidden? Were you part of the group that was hidden from the Red Cross when they came to visit the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I was in that room. The Red Cross came. They took us to the bakery, yes, "Take him and hide him." And we were there concealed from the Red Cross, and the Red Cross could not register us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, among the people who were detained in the same room with you, were there several members of the Cengic family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them? Were they taken out for exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They were. What connection it was or what was it, we only noticed in the room, "Get ready, you two, to be exchanged." And Cengic and his nephew left my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they taken out as a part of a larger exchange or were they exchanged in a separate exchange, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Separate exchange, smaller exchange. It went through a connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what the connection was or who arranged for them to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: On the basis of what we heard from -- Nezir Cengic's son was in the government in Sarajevo before the war and this son went to school together with Milosevic, so then this connection came into play and then they were exchanged from the KP Dom immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did any of the Cengics ever tell you that any prison staff or military commanders played a role in their exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When were you taken out of KP Dom for exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: In the month of July, from the KP Dom, we were transferred to Rudo for an exchange, 22 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I think it was July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What were you told was the reason you were being taken to Rudo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What reason were you given for being taken to Rudo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The reason was that we were going to Rudo from the KP Dom to be exchanged. We did not realise what the situation was, that there were Serbs from Rudo captured in Gorazde. And then by bus we were transferred from Foca to Rudo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Rudo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Six months in Rudo in the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you compare whether -- could you compare the conditions in the Rudo camp and the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were a bit poorer. The ground floor, no water, one lavatory. Five of us would have to line up and go to the lavatory. Bad conditions. Ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what you just described, was that at Rudo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Rudo, yes. The cultural centre, ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were at the KP Dom, were you ever beaten at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I was only beaten at the hospital in Foca. I am telling you the truth. I was not beaten anywhere else. Three prisons, two hospitals, in two and a half years. There was only fear, illness. I suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, did the detainees there tell you about beatings that had occurred before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, they did say that at first there were beatings and that there were people taken away. And when we came, we were told that we would not be taken out and not beaten. However, there was this wild exchange in my case. People were being taken out but they were not registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said you were told that you would not be beaten or exchanged. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The guard said so. Those requests of mine, the letters I wrote, he said, "(redacted), nothing doing, nothing will come out of that." And that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anybody assure you that you would not be beaten? Did anybody in authority say you would not be beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I wasn't sure. I was afraid. I was panic-stricken. How could I know what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While you were at the Rudo camp, did you receive medical treatment there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. I was in prison for three months. My situation -- my condition deteriorated. Everybody smoked. I don't smoke. This asthma. And I was being suffocated and then I was taken to the hospital in Rudo. Dr. Vera Rajak took me in and she treated me. They were humane. They were good to me. I had medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you finally registered with the Red Cross when you were at Rudo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: When we came to Rudo, on the next day the Red Cross came and then I registered with them there. Then they allowed me to write a message to my family saying that I was alive and where I was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that the first time you were able to contact your family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The first time after 22 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: From Rudo, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: After six months of prison in Rudo, we were taken during the night to Sarajevo Kula, the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: After six months of Rudo, of the prison in Rudo. I do not recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When were you finally released from prison, that is from Kula?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I was in Kula in prison for three months. There was a deterioration, in Kasindol I was also taken into hospital, two and a half years later I was exchanged in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you receive medical treatment when you were released in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me when they exchanged me, where I would go and whether I had family in Sarajevo. I said, "No. I want to go to hospital, to recuperate. I want to have my rib cage x-rayed to see whether something would have to be done again and whether I would have to receive further treatment." And that's the way it was. I was sent to the hospital Podhrastova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why did you ask to have your rib cage x-rayed? What did you expect was the problem?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: There was a problem. It hurt me. My ribs hurt me. However, they told me that only two ribs were broken. However, when they x-rayed me, I was in hospital for 15 days. And in the letter that was given to me when I was released, it said that there were four ribs that were broken and the fifth one was fractured a bit. You have this letter of release from hospital in Sarajevo, and please take a good look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment. The rib cage -- the rib injuries that you described, were those as a result of being beaten by Pero Elez in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Had you gotten an x-ray of those ribs at any point before you were released in Sarajevo in October of 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Kasindol, in the hospital, I was transferred to Kula because I was ill. And a doctor saw me and he said, "(redacted), tell me, quite freely: If they had beaten you, what is it that hurts you?" And I told him that they had beat me in the ribs. And he x-rayed me and then he sent me to hospital and I spent three months there on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question this way: While you were detained at KP Dom, did anybody take an x-ray of your ribs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you receive any treatment at KP Dom for the rib injuries that you got on the 2nd of October, 1992, while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. No. I only got injections and medicines when I would be all choked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: From your asthma?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Asthma, yes. Asthma, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the Witness shown ID282, and this is the medical record that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Is this the medical record of the treatment you received in Sarajevo upon your release in 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, this is my letter of release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And this is also the document, is it not, that you referred to as showing the x-rays of your broken ribs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead and take a look at this discharge certificate from Sarajevo, and you can see all these things in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution wishes to enter this exhibit into evidence as P282 and 282A, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P282, the other document will be P282A, and they will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are all our questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Very briefly, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I should like to continue along the lines of one of the last questions that my learned colleague had put. However, first I would like to wish the witness a good afternoon and I would like to introduce myself. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac and I am an attorney at law, one of the Defence counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I will have to ask you one more thing. Please do not answer my questions immediately, as soon as I put them, because we speak the same language. It is necessary for the interpreters to interpret this question first in order for everyone else in the courtroom to know the question that is being put and what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm sorry to say so, but you came in so far into that answer as it was still being translated that the interpreters, I think, had to gallop very hard to keep up with you. So you pause too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that in the KP Dom you did not get anything for your injuries except for injections and medicine. Did you complain to anyone specifically regarding your rib injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did you complain to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: To Dr. Aziz Torlak. And it is only a wet sheet that could save me and that would be bandaged around my ribs. I didn't have anything else to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you go to the prison clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: No. I could not stand on my own two feet for four months. They had to feed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After four months and after you managed to get on your own two feet, did you go to the prison clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did you go to see at the prison clinic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: There was this little male nurse. I forgot his name. He took us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you complain to him about your injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What did he tell you in response to that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He said that they would rather exchange a horse than me. What a shame.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you say how you sustained your injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I did not dare speak about that, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who gave you injections and medicines?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The male nurse. He brought them and our doctors administered them to me when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This nurse that you're speaking about, that you spoke of just now, that's the nurse of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to my learned colleague's question concerning your statement, when you said that Savo Todovic was warden of the KP Dom, you explained this, and my colleague also asked you whether Drs. Torlak or Karovic sent some requests to him. However, it is not quite clear after that, so I have to ask you now whether it is correct that in the statement that you gave to the OTP in 1998 you said the following: "I know that on my behalf, Dr. Aziz Torlak and Dr. Ibrahim Karovic wrote a request to Savo Todovic. They asked that I should be exchanged because I was very ill." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Correct. But nothing came out of this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me whether you also said that you were spared of any kind of work.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. As a patient, a sick person who had been beaten up, I was given a certificate that I was not forced to do any physical labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you also said that you knew the names of two guards. One was Burilo and the other was Matovic, who was a youngish man, medium height, with dark hair. He wore a military camouflage uniform and he was armed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I don't remember, given all that fear. I think they also had a pistol along with this guard's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So what you stated to the Prosecutor's office that this guard was in military camouflage uniform, that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I said "guard's uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the medical treatment you received. Do you know the name of Milivoje Milic, a guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. He is the only guard who let me open the window. He said, "(redacted), when I'm on duty, you can stand by the open window. When I'm on duty, I'll bring the nurse to administer injections to you," whereas the others would say, "Jump off the third floor, you balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So he even brought a doctor to see you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today during the examination-in-chief, you explained that you were beaten when you were leaving the hospital, going to the KP Dom. You said that this was done by the police. Was this the military police or some other police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: In hospital I was beaten by Pero Elez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that nobody beat you except for Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb police did. I don't know their names. When I was leaving the hospital, as I was walking downstairs, he hit me with a baton. And I held onto the railing. Had it not been for the railing, I would have fallen down. Three days later it was all black and blue, the place where he beat me with the baton, and he was kicking me in the ass all the time as I was going down. And I also fell and there was blood all over me. And he took a pistol and pointed it at me and he counted up to 10, and by the time he counted to 8, I came to and I managed to get up. And the other -- and when we got to the car, he put those other two in the car and he put me into the trunk, where there was dust and there were chains. Gentlemen, had there been a longer ride to the KP Dom, I would have suffocated all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why didn't you dare tell the police in Gorazde about this? Wasn't this the Muslim police that you gave this statement to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I said later that the first statement -- I mean, everything the way it was, later in Sarajevo. I said, in connection with everything I had to say -- please take a look at my papers. They're all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
