utterances.text: Sir, my colleague from the Office of the Prosecutor who was questioning you asked you why you did not talk about this incident in your first statement given to the police in Gorazde, and you explained that you were afraid to make such a statement. And now I am asking you whether, at the security station in Gorazde, this was the Muslim police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, that was the Muslim police. And two and a half years later, when I was exchanged in Sarajevo -- I mean, Rasevic took me to Gorazde, I got some rest and then I made statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were not afraid to mention Pero Elez in this statement, though.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, they asked me, "How do you know, (redacted), that Pero beat you?" And I said I knew that Pero came after the lady doctor and that he started beating me and she said, "Pero, in the name of your children, I ask you to stop beating them." And then -- oh, I'm sorry I even mentioned the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said, "Later I heard about the last name Elez." How come?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: When I was sent to Fojnica, I took the newspaper Dnevni Avaz, and then it said as if he had been killed. And then his family put a notice in Dvnevni Avaz, and I recognised him. I said this is the guy who beat me, a big guy with a beard, and it said "Pero Elez". And there is his father's name also. You can look at this document and you can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said during the examination-in-chief that he was portrayed as a hero.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: You can read it. You can read it and you can see what he did there and what he did in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you because, in your examination-in-chief, you said that he was portrayed as a hero.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Please, take a look at this document and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, just one thing. Dnevni Avaz, is that a Muslim newspaper or is that a newspaper that is published in the territory Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: This is a BH newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you once again, sir, about two policemen whom you mentioned, that they came to take you from hospital to the KP Dom and that they beat you. Were they military policemen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Ordinary policemen in uniform. When the doctor phoned, they came, and one of them kicked me and hit me with a baton.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We heard about this, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: If I have to tell you about it, I'm going to tell you about it right now. And you can go to Foca and you can go to the hospital and talk to the doctor and she can tell you exactly the way this went. I want the truth to be known and I came here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, please. I am not bringing into question what you are saying. I'm just interested in something else.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm not challenging any of the things that you are saying. I'm not saying you're not telling the truth. Just tell me whether they were military policemen or not. I'm not bringing into question what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: They were not military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave in 1998 to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said the following. I don't have to repeat all of this. You talked about this incident with a certain Pero and you said, "When he beat us, he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. did not have weapons." And then you say, "The doctor called the police. Two military policemen came. Pero in the meantime left."

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Pero went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Two military policemen came." And then at the next paragraph, again you said, "The military policemen handed us over to the prison staff." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The policemen handed us over, but that fear, I certainly could not see whether they were military or whether they had ordinary uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also said the prison staff that was present wore camouflage uniforms. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that what I read from your statement given to the OTP, that the prison staff present there wore camouflage uniforms, you say that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After Room 15, what room were you in, if you may remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Later, we were transferred to two rooms. I think it was number 30 and number 20. As people left for plum picking, others were brought in. So during that year in the KP Dom in Foca, I was in three different rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First you said 15 and then you said 20 and 30. Room number 30 does not exist. Could you please focus a bit? Which room was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Well, you tend to forget. There was 25, 20, 18. Those were the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please tell us, from Room 15, were you transferred to the right-hand wing of the prison complex?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: The left-hand wing, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And all the three rooms that you were in were in the left wing of the prisoners' quarters?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, left, up there with those birches.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the clinic and the prison hospital were in that wing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes, but below.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Safet Avdic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He was in the same room, former director.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How long was he with you in Room 15?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: About six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So six months after your arrival on the 1st of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: He left to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: From Room 15?

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That is the end of your evidence. Thank you for giving that evidence. You are now free to leave. I suggest you wait a moment while the blinds are being lowered so you can leave without being seen by the public.

utterances.speaker: FWS-146
utterances.text: Thank you, too. All the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Smith, we are up to 120, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What are the protective measures for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: A pseudonym and facial.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in the document that is being shown to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. In front of you is a sheet of paper. On the top of that sheet of paper is a name and date of birth. Is that your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We believe that we did have copies but the case manager has just gone to make a few. We have copies now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that it's already admitted into evidence this morning. It was when the witness came that had the name. It was on my desk and I'm afraid I thought it was he, and I put it into evidence before the witness came in and gave a different name and didn't realise it. So it is already in evidence as Exhibit 427.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is actually a different version because it does have the date of birth of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. We will have another one. It will be Exhibit 429 and it will be P429, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, during and prior to April, 1992, were you a career JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was -- what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was -- who was the fuel intended for? What was the purpose of this fuel depot?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: That -- there was no fuel in that depot. Preparations were under way so that the fuel, which would subsequently fed into the cisterns and used by the Muslim People's Army and the United Nations, their forces which were in east Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was this depot fenced?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what buildings and structures were in this compound area?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: There was a prefabricated building housing the command for the supply and feeding of fuel into cisterns, with an automatic system for the loading, unloading, showing the exact state of fuel and the quantity available in the depot. Then there were also storerooms which were dug in and used for things such as oils, oil derivatives, oil derivatives which were in cisterns, in barrels, in cannisters, and there was also an open warehouse used to distribute fuel, that is to pour it into containers or into smaller containers, from one to 20 litres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to clarify a matter. In your previous answer you said that the fuel was intended to be fed into the cisterns used by the Muslim People's Army. Did you say that or did you say the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: JNA. Not the Muslim army; the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The answer went on to say, "and the United Nations." I don't know whether that was intended as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the fuel was to be used for the United Nations as well, as well as the JNA. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case, because that depot belonged to the federal agencies of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, which in December turned it over to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where is the compound in relation to the main road between Foca and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: It is eight kilometres away from Foca, on the road to Gorazde, and three kilometres from Ustikolina, towards Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far was the command building within this compound from the main gate?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: The command was 10, maybe 12 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how big was the compound, approximately, the length and width?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: It was about 800 metres long and the average width was 100 or, at some places, 200 metres, depending, from the gate and then onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as of April 1992, how many soldiers did you have under your command?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: I had 14 soldiers and 4 civilians, civilians working for the Yugoslav People's Army. The soldiers were regular JNA soldiers doing their regular military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were they of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when were you transferred to this fuel depot?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: I was transferred after the first blockade of Sarajevo. It was on the 6th of April. No. Excuse me. I was transferred in November 1991, and that depot was the depot of the federal agencies. So they had begun the process of turning it over, and on the 6th of April, after the blockade of Sarajevo, the first one, I refused to go to work in Ustikolina. But from my command, my command warned me that I had to go. And no sooner did I talk to them on the phone than - with the men in charge in my command - than the military police arrived to the house where I lived. And after that, I went to the command, and for three days attempts were being made for me to leave Sarajevo to get to Ustikolina. I tried to reach Ustikolina, taking the direction of Trnovo, but it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ordered to go back to the Pilipovici fuel depot?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: I did not get an order. I was taken by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you intend not to go back to Pilipovici in April?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Because I had already sensed and heard in the media that the situation had reached a critical point in that part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in any event, you were escorted back to Pilipovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you resumed your command position there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At this time was there a JNA base in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how far from Pilipovici is Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the function of this JNA base?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: It was the third depot of ammunition and explosive devices. They had their warehouses in two places, and the command in the centre itself of Ustikolina, right next to the mosque. Its function, the function of the depot, was the logistical supply of ammunition, mines, and explosive devices, the supply for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in compliance with orders received from Sarajevo, from the 777th Rear Base of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how many troops were based at this warehouse complex in Ustikolina, including the command centre and the two warehouses?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was not directly subordinate to the commander who was the commander in the 3rd depot. At no time did I insist on getting a number of soldiers, because the formations in former barracks were all a military secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Even though you don't know the number of the troops, were the troops of mixed ethnicity that were attached to this base?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Until January, there were regular troops of the Yugoslav People's Army, and those were lads doing their military service. In January, in addition to their number, a significant number of reservists of one ethnic origin turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what ethnic group was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "they turned up," what did they do when they got there? Did they become part of the troops at that base?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: According to what I could see and feel, some of them were -- that is, those reservists who came to the barracks had been supplied with clothing, footwear, weapons, and some of them stayed in the barracks and others headed for other places on the basis of the assignments that were not known to me; that is, I did not know their assignments and I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know about the arrival of these extra men to the JNA base in Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: I know it because logistically I -- it was this depot which was to support me logistically, and pursuant to the orders of the command in Sarajevo, I was getting my food supplies, ammunition, weapons, and all derivatives from that depot, so that I came practically every day, once or twice even, depending on the situation there. And all the orders that came from Sarajevo came to that depot, because they had a fax machine and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you notice whether or not the Muslims that were attached to that JNA base, whether they started to leave in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: They started to leave on the basis of somebody's orders. I do not know whose. But by January the 15th, not a single Muslim reservist was to be found in that base.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many Muslims left that base?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Whatever I tell you won't be the accurate figure, but quite a number of them left. I wasn't really fully abreast of it all, but Muslims did not turn up any more; that is, you call a man and you see that this Muslim is not there, that those names are gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the command structure at the JNA base in Ustikolina in January, do you know what ethnicity that was, if it was one particular type, or was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: It was mixed. The commander was a Serb, and in depots there were Serbs from Bosnia, Serbs from Serbia. But by and large, they were all active military persons in the Yugoslav People's Army, and the structure Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was determined by the command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the command structure was mixed. Did Muslim commanders stay in Ustikolina or did they leave, at this time in January?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Active-duty military did not leave, because they dared not, because they would be brought before a court martial, as at that time the Yugoslav People's Army was still in all the barracks in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it had not yet been condemned by anyone as a monoethnic army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the Muslims that were attached to this base that left in January 1992, where did they go and why did they go?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: According to stories which I heard from active-duty military down there, they disagreed with the policy of the Yugoslav People's Army, and they went to their native places and some of them organised groups and groupings, and I do not have any detailed knowledge about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In early April 1992, did any civilians approach you at the fuel depot and ask you for some protection within the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: As early as the 8th of April, a large number of civilians began to arrive from the direction of Foca, began to move from the direction of Foca towards Ustikolina. And when arriving at the gate, people began first to speak to soldiers, and then soldiers approached me directly to see if we could accommodate the refugees in the depot because people still trusted the Yugoslav People's Army, that there would be no killings and that that army would provide them with logistic support, that is food in the first place and perhaps a roof somewhere to sleep, so that they could go on either to Gorazde or some other place, that is take some other road which was still passable in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly, did they tell you why they left, why they left Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: They said because an attack had taken place on some villages around Foca, and because these people had been expelled. And during the war, it happened, if the news reaches you that somebody, some three kilometres away, is coming to kill you and expel you, then everybody is on the run so as to avoid finding themselves in the same predicament as those that had been attacked already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think you said that the first civilians that approached you was about the 8th of April. Did the numbers increase throughout April?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on the 26th of April, 1992, the compound was taken over by other forces?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, and that was Easter, the White Eagles paramilitary formations took over the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the maximum number of people that you had in the compound prior to the 26th of April that were seeking protection?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the night. Until the 26th, there were never less than 300, and at times, it was as many as 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during the day, did a number of these people leave the compound and then come back at night? Was that a pattern that was developing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: Some went on towards Gorazde, and some, those who were nearest, whose houses were nearest the barracks, they would go in the morning and return at night-time because they thought it was safer for them to be in the barracks at night than in their houses, in case of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you know the ethnicity of these people that were seeking protection?

utterances.speaker: FWS-120
utterances.text: The majority of them were Muslims, 99 per cent. However, one of the first to seek protection was a man of Serb origin, and he was in the depot together with all the other refugees throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's probably a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of February, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
